1.pericope_label: Moreover he said unto me, Son of man, eat that thou findest; eat this roll, and go speak unto the house of Israel
debates: Where the chapter division should fall
How the sweetness relates to the bitterness of the message
What the eating of the roll signifies
outliers: Gill reports that Junius and Tremellius make the first fifteen verses part of the preceding chapter, and Henry that some translators join them to it as belonging to the same vision

Ellicott infers from a later verse that this prophet had the same bitterness another seer reports, though he does not say so; Calvin holds instead that the prophet forgot the sorrow in the book because the justice of God prevailed over his humanity
Henry reads the eating as study and application, a rule for preachers; Calvin reads it as speaking from the inmost affection of the heart, against those whose fluency is only ostentation
Clarke holds the eating must have passed in vision rather than in fact
themes: A roll to be ruminated on as a beast chews the cud
Fluent tongues whose vanity God makes a laughing stock
A prophet who pitied his people and subscribed to the judgment anyway
The first part of ministerial work called usually pleasant

4.pericope_label: For thou art not sent to a people of a strange speech and of an hard language, but to the house of Israel
debates: How the conditional clause should be rendered
What all the house of Israel means
Why the comparison with foreign nations is made
outliers: Calvin reports three renderings of the clause, from Jerome as a supposition of sending, from others as a form of swearing rendered affirmatively, and from others as saying they would have heard had he not been sent, and rejects all three for his own, that but for the difference of speech God would rather have sent him elsewhere
Ellicott and Wesley both restrict all to the generality, Ellicott naming saints who were exceptions even then and Wesley saying the far greater part though not every particular person

Calvin reports the view that the comparison animates the prophet, since a mission to nations whose speech he did not know would have been a complete obstacle; Clarke reads it as reproach, that even those nations would more likely have hearkened
Gill and Calvin agree the refusal is aimed past the prophet at God, so that the people rejected the Lord and his words rather than the man
themes: A rule that ministers should not heap up their own comments
Marginal readings called very nervous and very correct
A people who would embrace the fables of any impostor who poured darkness upon them
Servants asked why they should mind being valued as God is valued

8.pericope_label: As an adamant harder than flint have I made thy forehead: fear them not, neither be dismayed at their looks, though they be a rebellious house
debates: What the adamant is
Whether hearing precedes reception in the heart
Why the obstinacy of the people is named to the prophet
outliers: Gill derives the name from its being unconquerable by hammer or fire and reports that Bochart took it for the stone jewellers polish gems with; Ellicott says simply that it is the diamond, and makes the point that as the diamond cuts flint so the words of the prophet should cut through their resistance
Calvin holds the terms inverted, since we must perceive with the ear before we receive in the heart, and says those philosophize with more subtlety than truth who make the interior hearing come first
Calvin gives two reasons, that the prophet is strengthened lest he despair at contending with stones, and that had he hoped for more fruit the very ease might have made him negligent
Ellicott marks that God sends him not to my people but to thy people, refusing to own them in their present state while reminding the prophet that he is one of them
themes: A face that could not be looked out of countenance
A word taken from the figure of horned animals in their contests
A prophet called more verbose than others because he wrote for exiles whose language had degenerated with their faith
Exhortations still needed by a man already given unconquered fortitude

12.pericope_label: Then the spirit took me up, and I heard behind me a voice of a great rushing, saying, Blessed be the glory of the LORD from his place
debates: Whether the transport was bodily or in vision
What the place from which the glory is blessed is
What the agitation of the prophet amounted to
outliers: Gill insists the transport was real and bodily, expressly against Kimchi, and compares the catching away of Philip; Ellicott holds it was done in vision like the later instances; Clarke reports three explanations from Calmet and says only that the going was real
The place is read three ways: Calvin takes it for the Temple, Wesley for a coming down from heaven, Clarke for the throne of glory

Calvin distinguishes this from the ecstasy profane men ascribe to their own prophets, who were deprived of self-control, holding that the prophets of God were of a sedate and composed mind and that visible marks were graven on this one to gain reverence for his teaching
Calvin notes that the word for the touching wings is rendered by some of wings striking or engaging in conflict, and holds that the kissing signifies conjunction
themes: Wings said to kiss each one its sister
A benediction set against the murmuring of a people who thought themselves harshly used
A command that was sweet and a performance that is bitter
A man well known to his friends separated from common life to represent something celestial

15.pericope_label: Then I came to them of the captivity at Telabib, that dwelt by the river of Chebar, and I sat where they sat, and remained there astonished among them seven days
debates: What the seven days of silence were for
Whether the clause about sitting should be read of sitting or seeing
Whether the day was a sabbath
outliers: Ellicott takes the seven days for the set time of mourning and a sympathy with the people; Clarke reads them as discipline, God withholding revelation until the bitterness of the prophet was subdued; Calvin and Wesley make it simple waiting for instructions not yet given
Ellicott finds the clause so difficult that it has produced variant readings and a marginal correction, and proposes changing the vowel pointing so that it reads that he saw where they sat
Henry thinks it very probable that this day and the day of the vision were both sabbaths; Gill allows that some think so but holds it neither certain nor a necessary inference

Calvin dismisses as frivolous the view that the prophet sought solitude like a monk lest he contract a stain, holding that he had never removed from his people but was drawn out of ordinary intercourse by the vision
themes: A settlement chosen both to keep captives in and to make them defend it
A name read as a heap of new fruit by one version and as the hill of grief by another
An ambassador chosen by a king before his instructions are given him
Raptures called not the daily bread of the children of God

17.pericope_label: Son of man, I have made thee a watchman unto the house of Israel: therefore hear the word at my mouth, and give them warning from me
debates: What the watchman office amounts to
Whether the minister may condemn or absolve
What death is threatened
outliers: Gill takes the watchman in an ecclesiastical sense, the Targum rendering it teacher, and makes it the same office as that of bishops or overseers; Calvin reaches the same identification from the word bishop itself, and adds that pastors must be endued with superior gifts and not live as private men

Calvin denies that any mortal may condemn or absolve at his own discretion, holding that God does not resign that power when he sends out his servants, since there is one lawgiver who can save and destroy
Gill holds the threatened death not corporeal only but eternal, the wages and issue of sin unless grace prevent
Clarke adds that the word must be received at the mouth of God, since God will have no more of human creeds than of traditions taught for divine doctrine
themes: Watchmen of cities who give the time of night and notice of danger
Sermons called not bread from heaven but dry mouldy crusts
Men who take their tithes to the last penny while those they watch over perish
A boast of apostolical authority called vain in men who do not the work of apostles

19.pericope_label: Again, When a righteous man doth turn from his righteousness, and commit iniquity, and I lay a stumblingblock before him, he shall die
debates: Whether a truly righteous man can fall away
What the stumbling-block is
What the impious way adds to impiety
outliers: Gill denies the words can mean one truly righteous or justified by the righteousness of Christ, and takes them of a man righteous only by an outward reformation of his own; Clarke calls that reading absurd, since self-righteousness is itself a fall, and holds that real righteousness of heart and life is meant and that such a man may fall from grace and perish everlastingly; Calvin raises the same difficulty from the incorruptible seed of the Spirit and the adoption that is without repentance
Ellicott sets the theological question aside and takes the passage simply as representing the upright man exposed to temptation, holding both terms comparative

Clarke and Wesley read the stumbling-block as permission rather than act, God being repeatedly represented as doing what he only permits; Ellicott takes it for anything at which people stumble, whether intended so or designed for their highest good
Calvin offers a distinction between impiety as the inward wickedness of the heart and the impious way as the outward life comprehending all actions
themes: A blessing that returns to the man who gave it when the house proves unworthy
Watchmen called dumb dogs if they keep silence
A word used oftener by this prophet than by all other writers of the Old Testament together
A saying that the pastor kills the man by being silent

22.pericope_label: And the hand of the LORD was there upon me; and he said unto me, Arise, go forth into the plain, and I will there talk with thee
debates: What the hand of the Lord means
Why the prophet is shut in his house
Whether the order of commands is a change of plan
outliers: Gill reports the Targum taking the hand for the spirit of prophecy but prefers a fresh impulse of the Spirit; Calvin calls the exposition that makes it the prophetic office cold and takes it for power, the agitation of the Spirit

Clarke reads the shutting up as hiding for the present; Ellicott offers either a private beginning to the prophecies or a further period of silence and meditation; Wesley makes it a sign foresignifying the shutting up of the people in Jerusalem

Calvin answers the objection that God trifles with his servant by sending him out and then shutting him in, holding that the alternation confirmed his authority since God governed his tongue for speech and silence alike
Henry reads the retirement as accommodation to a man not yet convinced that his sender could bear him out
themes: A commission whose first work seems not proportionable to the pomp of the call
A plain chosen because the glory needed room to manifest itself
A prophet who supposed he was sent out to speak at once and was mistaken
Visions no longer expected, and a favour said to be nothing inferior

25.pericope_label: But thou, O son of man, behold, they shall put bands upon thee, and shall bind thee with them, and thou shalt not go out among them
debates: Whether the bands are literal or figurative
Why the dumbness is ascribed to God rather than to the people
What the reopening of the mouth refers to
outliers: Clarke and Wesley take the bands literally, of confinement by his countrymen; Ellicott argues firmly for the figurative sense, since there is no trace of imprisonment in the book, it is unlikely under Nebuchadnezzar and impossible under the administration of Daniel, and a later laying on of bands must be figurative; Gill offers three possibilities without choosing, and Calvin allows both the metaphorical and the literal and leaves the choice free

Ellicott notes that the silence is attributed not to the rebellious house who brought it about but to God, whose providence was its ultimate cause; Calvin reconciles the two, since the people rejected prophecy and God then deprived them of it as unworthy
Ellicott refers the reopening to the later verses where after the destruction of the city the mouth of the prophet is shut no longer, and takes the messages of this book to begin at that point
Calvin holds the ceasing of all prophecy to be a sign of divine vengeance, since when instruction is removed it is as if God hid his face and turned his back
themes: A prophet taken for a madman by his motions and gestures
An apostle whose mouth was open and heart enlarged while the bowels of his hearers were straitened
A God who rises early and keeps watch while it is yet night before withdrawing his teaching
An embassy that opens with an insult where ambassadors usually try courtesy
